blocks.text: $D_k(i,j)$ нь завсрын оройг зөвхөн 1..$k$-ээс сонгосон хамгийн бага өртөг. Эхлэл/төгсгөл нь тэр хязгаарт заавал орох албагүй. $k$-гүй хамгийн сайн зам өмнөх $D_{k-1}(i,j)$; $k$-г дайрвал $i$→$k$ ба $k$→$j$ хэсэгт сална.

en.title: Floyd–Warshall — all-pairs distances, negative cycles and paths
en.summary: Implement intermediate-set phases, full matrix traces, parallel edges, pair-specific negative-cycle influence and finite path reconstruction.

content.text: When queries have different sources and targets, preprocess all pair distances. Floyd–Warshall starts a matrix
from direct edges, then permits intermediate vertices one at a time. It is simple for small $n$, but cubic time makes it unsuitable for large $n$.

blocks.caption: Five undirected vertices. Matrix rows are sources and columns are targets.

content.text: for the empty walk, direct-edge weights for edges, and INF otherwise. Keep the minimum of parallel edges. A zero weight is still an edge, so do not use
as a presence test. Do not erase a negative self-loop with zero: the general version sets zero first, then minimizes with input edges.

blocks.text: Initial matrix from direct edges. ∞ means no walk found yet.

sections.title: Intermediate-vertex phases and the outer k loop

blocks.text: $D_k(i,j)$ is the minimum cost when internal vertices may only come from 1..$k$; endpoints need not lie in that set. A best path avoiding $k$ has cost $D_{k-1}(i,j)$; one using $k$ splits into $i$→$k$ and $k$→$j$.

$D_k(i,j)=\min(D_{k-1}(i,j),D_{k-1}(i,k)+D_{k-1}(k,j))$. Skip the second choice if either segment is unreachable. Without negative cycles, remove unhelpful cycles so a best path needs to use $k$ at most once, proving the recurrence.

content.text: Keep $k$ as the outermost loop. A phase updates every $i$,$j$ using the preceding phase. Without negative cycles

, so the $i$→$k$ and $k$→$j$ values remain unchanged within the phase, permitting an in-place matrix. A single pass with $i$,$j$ outside and $k$ inside loses this invariant and can miss multi-edge paths.

blocks.text: With negative cycles, do not call every computed numeric entry a shortest distance. The first program below is the simple nonnegative case; a later extension separately handles negative-cycle influence.

Print −1 if unreachable, otherwise the distance. Nonnegative finite distances cannot conflict with the −1 sentinel output.

The Floyd constructor sets diagonal zero and other entries INF. add minimizes both directions. A simple shortest path costs at most ($n$−1)×10⁹, and adding two finite segments fits ll and INF=2⁶⁰. Skipping sums involving INF preserves reachability semantics as well as arithmetic safety.
Distances use ll and indices int; a 500-city path can exceed 32 bits.
The size constructor initializes empty-walk diagonal entries.

sections.title: Negative cycles invalidate only pairs with both reachability conditions

content.text: In a directed graph with negative weights each pair has three statuses: unreachable, finite minimum, or unbounded below. If
<0, a negative closed walk is reachable from and returns to $k$. Pair ($i$,$j$) can exploit it precisely when $i$ reaches $k$ and $k$ reaches $j$.
finite. This is pair-specific influence, unlike a single-source
. Store flags separately instead of overwriting $d$ with −INF while checking reachability.

blocks.text: In the eight-vertex example from the Bellman–Ford lesson, 1 can reach cycle 2→3→2, but the cycle cannot get to 5. Thus (1,5)=7 and (1,1)=0 remain finite, while (1,4)=−INF. The cycle at 6,7, unreachable from 1, still makes (6,7)=−INF. Pairs (2,1),(2,5) are unreachable, not −INF.

Without negative cycles the zero-diagonal phase proof still applies. With negative cycles numeric estimates can become extremely negative and must not be printed as actual minima. The general code uses numeric answers only for unaffected pairs and prints an unbounded status otherwise.

blocks.text: Why does the floor preserve finite answers? With $n$≤300 and |$w$|≤10⁹, a simple path has absolute cost at most 3×10¹¹, far from −2⁶⁰. A walk that drops below the floor requires a negative cycle, so its pair is marked bad. A simple negative cycle also has magnitude bounded by $n$×10⁹ and can be detected on a negative diagonal without approaching the floor. Capping does not erase reachability.

Input $n$ $m$ q, then $m$ DIRECTED triples a b $w$ and q pairs a b. Require 0≤$n$≤300,$m$≤100000,q≤20000 and |$w$|≤10⁹, with $m$=q=0 for $n$=0. Insert both directions for undirected data. Distance and influence preprocessing each take $O(n³)$, still $O(n³)$ total. Three tables use $O(n^2)$ space. Status/distance lookup is $O(1)$, but printing a path adds up to $O(n)$ work; include total output size over q queries.
Check yourself: why is $k$ outermost? Is a zero edge absent? Is ($i$,$j$) affected when $i$ reaches a negative cycle but the cycle cannot reach $j$? Can one cycle invalidate every pair automatically?

Answers: to preserve the intermediate-set phase; no; no; no. Independently enumerate small simple paths and negative elementary cycles to verify all three statuses and reconstructed costs. Test self-loops, parallel/zero edges, disconnected negative cycles, singletons and unreachable pairs.
Core problem for mastery
Shortest Routes II: use the first undirected nonnegative program; check parallel minima, unreachable −1 and diagonal zero.
Independent practice and extensions
Shortest Routes: for a single source with large $n$, compare Dijkstra instead of allocating n² distances.
Flight Discount: a one-discount state is not an ordinary all-pairs distance.
Investigation: shortest-path counts and edge statistics need more than distances.
Course Schedule: dependency ordering is not a weighted shortest-path objective.
High Score: after negating weights, verify both source and target reachability around the cycle.
